utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to greet everyone here in this courtroom, Mr. Mundis, Mr. Kruger. We would also like to greet the Defence counsel here today as well as the accused. I see that two of the accused are victims of the flu epidemic. I hope this won't affect the other accused present today in the courtroom. I would also like to greet everyone else in the courtroom. Let me first give the floor to the registrar. We need two IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. So several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered thank you Witness Salem Cerenic. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 495, while the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 496. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm first going to read out a decision. I'm going to read it out slowly for it to be interpreted properly, without any mistakes. This is a decision on the application made by the parties to be heard about matters related to the -- to procedural matters. At the hearings of the 14th, 15th, and 19th of March, 2007, the parties invited the Chamber to hold a meeting on matters related to the proceedings. The Chamber has decided to hold a hearing on these matters this Thursday, 22nd of March, 2007, at 9.00 in Courtroom II. Let me add that because Courtroom II is so small, and it is free because Dragomir Milosevic Chamber is currently in Sarajevo, because the courtroom is so small we won't be able to accommodate the accused in that particular courtroom, but the accused will be represented by their counsel, of course. The Trial Chamber notes, however, that during the hearings of the 14th, 15th, and 19th of March, 2007, the Prosecution, as well as some Defence counsel, have already expressed part of their concerns, and therefore this -- it will not be necessary to repeat this. The Chamber believes that this hearing should be held without the accused being present since only matters of a purely technical and procedural nature will be raised at the meeting. For the hearing to be as fruitful and constructive as possible, the Trial Chamber would like to invite the party to submit a list of the points they want to discuss during the hearing, and they should do so by tomorrow, 11.00 a.m. The Trial Chamber invites the Defence teams to get together in order for them to submit a single list common to all Defence counsel. On the basis of these two lists the Trial Chamber will set the agenda for the meeting, and this agenda will be announced to the parties tomorrow afternoon at the beginning of the hearing. The Trial Chamber would like to inform the Prosecution and the Defence that each of them will have a maximum of 60 minutes to make their respective submissions. Let me specify that 60 minutes for the Defence means 60 minutes for the -- all the Defence teams taken together. We don't have time to dedicate six hours to this matters. For the Defence -- therefore, it's 60 minutes for the Defence. So let me summarise. We will have a hearing on Thursday morning at 9.00 in Courtroom II. And that was this decision that I wanted to deliver orally here. Let me say that, as far as I'm concerned, when I read the transcript of last Thursday and I listened to what I had said, I identified 22 mistakes, 22 corrections that had to be made, errors, omissions that could distort the meaning of what I said. I will issue an order about these 22 corrections that should be made, and I will ask the registry to make sure that the transcript in French is true to the recording, and of course the English translation, it also to reflect what I said in French. I will issue an order in that respect in the next few days. Let me add one more thing, one last thing to avoid any misunderstanding. When the Trial Chamber issues a decision, this is a decision issued by the three Judges. Theoretically any of us, any of the three Judges could read this decision because it's a common decision. However, when a Judge puts a question, he's -- only the Judge who asks the question is involved, and when a Judge makes a submission it's his own personal submission. So you have to make a difference between a decision rendered by the Trial Chamber and a question or a submission made by a Judge on his own behalf. As an example, I would give you what I said previously. What I've just said I said on my own behalf, but the judgement I rendered on behalf of the three Judges. We have a number of witnesses this afternoon. I see that we have a lot of people in the public gallery. These witnesses we will hear will have protective measures granted to them; but, however, the public in the public gallery will be able to follow the proceedings. But let me say that these witnesses will benefit from the following protective measures: Pseudonym and distortion of the -- facial distortion. We'll have the witnesses brought in. We'll roll the blinds down and then we'll ask the witness to make the solemn declaration. Afterwards, we'll raise the blinds again and then the hearing and the testimony will start. I will ask the usher to roll down the blinds in order for the first witness to be able to enter the courtroom. Mr. Mundis, you have -- you wanted to make a three-minute submission about the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. In light of the fact that we ran a little long yesterday, I would like in private session just to outline very quickly where we expect or hope to be going this week with respect to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, we are in open session, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: -- nobody outside the courtroom can see your face and your name cannot be recognised. What I'm going to ask you is don't mention any names of any family members or of acquaintances of you unless I ask you to do so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. Now, first of all, could you tell the Court during 1993, is it correct that you were living outside Vares? The town of Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the outskirts of the town of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that at some stage during 1993, because your husband was away on business --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Excuse me. At some point you said that there was a voice distortion granted but we don't have any voice distortion. We only have facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry. That's my mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, sorry, did you understand that I had made a mistake, that your voice is not being distorted outside the courtroom? Witness, is it correct -- I'll just repeat the previous question. Is it correct that during 1993 you were alone -- living alone at your house because your husband was away on business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And during the evenings, who came to stay with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My younger sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that shortly before the 23rd of October, 1993, you and your sister moved to the house of your parents in the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What caused you to move to your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in our municipality there were two flags. There was one Yugoslav flag and one Croatian flag. This Croatian flag was hoisted when the Croats took over in Vares, and two days later or, rather, after the attack on Vares they put the Yugoslavia flag down and only the Croatian flag was left, and that made me feel suspicious, and I said to my sister, "Let's go to our parents' house." And we spent two nights down there until Vares was attacked on the 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, before coming to that day, prior to that period, prior to the 23rd of October [sic], 1993, were there any check-points, military check-points, in the vicinity of where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout Vares there were check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And which -- from which army were these check-points or by which army's personnel were they being manned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew. Everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how did you know? From what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew that they took over power in Vares, and they had insignia. They had the chequer-board emblem on their uniforms, on their caps. They wore Croatian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, if we could move to the morning of the 23rd of October [sic], 1993. Can you tell the Court what happened at the house of your father? And I will stop you after the departure of the first group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may just correct the transcript. I referred at page 11, line 2, to the 23rd of November. I mean the 23rd of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 23rd, in the morning, that was the 23rd of November, we got up -- in actual fact we were awake at 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: November or October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: November. November. The month of November, not October. I'm sorry. I'm so confused now. They came at 6.00 in the morning. They knocked at the door, and I opened the door. My father had gotten up already. He was in the bathroom. When I opened the door I saw three Croat soldiers. They asked whether there were any men in the house, and I said only our old father, who was sick. They actually asked for his ID, and he showed them his ID, and they saw what his age was, and they said that he should come with them. He just needed to wash his face, to comb his hair, but they didn't let him. They just let him put on his coat. And then we beseeched them to let our father go. He had had two heart attacks. He was an old man, 74 years old. They were clamouring, and they didn't let him wash his face or get dressed properly, and they told us that we shouldn't leave the house, that we should stay inside, and that they'd be back. However, when they took our father out of the house, and we looked through the window, and I think that there were three soldiers in front of every house and every apartment building. They were all over the place. There were some people outside only their underwear. They were hitting them with rifle butts, kicking them. They were doing all sorts of things to them. They were being taken to a camp that was at the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And when you say they were doing all sorts of things to them, could you just, for the record, tell the Court who do you mean by "they" who were doing these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croat army. The HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, madam, do you know where your father was taken, or did you find out subsequently where he was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took him to the camp at the secondary school centre in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the name of that secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Goran Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may move into private session for the next portion of the witness's testimony, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll move into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, after these soldiers had left, did you then remain in your house, you and your sister and your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And where did you flee to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We fled to a married couple. They were Croats, actually, Catholics, and we spent two days with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was this in the town of Vares still?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And after two days, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After two days the man that we stayed with came and said that everything was over and that we could go home. However, when we arrived we saw that not everything was over and we started to flee again but didn't know where, and then an elderly married couple, they were also Croats, but they allowed us to stay with them, an old man and woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Until when did you stay with this old man and woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I see. In light of what we were talking about previously, the date of the -- of the incidents you previously described to the Court, if this took place on the 1st of November, do you want to reconsider your answer that you gave previously, whether it was the 23rd of October or 23rd of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know it was the 1st of November when it was All Saints Day, so I got confused. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, your father -- while you were staying with this second Croat couple, did your father join you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, six days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say six days later, six days from the date of his arrest or another date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about the conditions under which he had been held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he told us what they slept on, that they were cold. They had no blankets. They had nothing, and that they beat them. And when a Croat would enter, one of the soldiers of the HVO, at the door they had to put their heads down not to see who was coming into the room. And when they beat them, they all had to keep their heads well down. They mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, madam, on the 1st of November or All Saints Day 1993, what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A young man came to fetch us. He was a Croat, a Catholic. And he took us with a car to the UNPROFOR headquarters, and that's where they protected people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When were you able to return to your house in Vares -- or outside Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days later when the BH army entered Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did you find at your house? In what condition or state was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my father's house was intact, but my house was destroyed and everything taken out of it. Just the big pieces of furniture were left in the house. Everything else was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for a final portion of the evidence, if we may just move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll move back into private session briefly, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kruger. Now to the Defence, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, madam. We have no questions for this witness. We wish to thank her for coming here to give her evidence. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Stojic Defence also has no questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of General Praljak also has no questions for this witness and we thank the witness for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a very short explanation, because I think that something was left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to try and clarify one point. When you spoke about the events that took place before what happened to you and while you were here, you said on the municipality in Vares the Yugoslav and Croatian flag were hoisted and that the Yugoslav flag was taken down, and that on the basis of that occurrence, you thought that some unpleasant things might happen. Now, I'd just like to ask you, are you quite sure that it was a Yugoslav flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I suppose so, because there could have been no other flag on the municipality building because it was still Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In October 1993? Well, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I only have one question to put to you. It's a follow-up question following the one put to you by Ms. Alaburic, a question related to the Yugoslav flag. In 1993, your country was independent and had its own flag. It was not the flag of the former Yugoslavia anymore. So are you mixing up this when you are talking about the Yugoslav flag? Are you mixing it up with the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you mix these things up in your mind or is it something that is not very specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I have mixed it up. I'm not quite sure at any rate. Perhaps in my memory. Perhaps I haven't got a good memory for flags. I don't know. I'm not quite sure, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for this answer. No additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam, on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues I'd like to thank you -- oh, wait a minute. My fellow Judge has a question to put to you. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a very small question, madam. You have told us how and why you moved to your parents' house. Can you tell us where you were living before you went there? And I wonder if that's something that can be named in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in my own house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was that house also located in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vares, but a little further away, the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No additional questions? Very well. Let me take the floor again then. Madam, thank you very much for coming here for the Prosecution, to testify in this case. On behalf of my colleagues I wish you a very safe trip home. Before you leave the courtroom, I'll ask the usher to roll down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Usher will bring the second witness. For the second witness we have one hour for the Prosecution and one hour for the Defence. Protective measures had been requested for that witness. We'll grant -- we'll proceed the same way as with the previous witness, pseudonym and facial distortion, and we'll go into closed session when we deal with some specific events, just as with the previous witness. Mr. Mundis, any concerns about this way of going about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No. I don't think there will be a problem. I'm just awaiting Mr. Scott's appearance through the door since he's scheduled to take the next witness, but he did -- he did send me an e-mail and say he's on his way, so hopefully ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Mr. Scott follows these proceedings with great care. I'm sure he noticed that this witness just left the courtroom, so I'm sure he'll show up very soon. But not to waste any more time, we'll bring in the next witness. I'm being told by the registrar that the witness is not here. In order not to waste any time, we'll have the break now. It's five past 3.00. We will have a 20-minute break and we'll resume in 20 minutes, and this will give enough time for Mr. Scott to arrive in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 3.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resume. We are running late because we were waiting for the witness, who has finally arrived. With regard to the protective measures, is there anything new, any new development, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. I regret the delay, but because of the -- because of the ruling and protective measures of course we needed to talk to the witness to see if that would be -- if she was agreeable to proceed on that basis, and, yes. Again, just to confirm for the record, it will be a pseudonym, facial image distortion, and private session as to any sensitive testimony. That's my understanding. On that basis, we're prepared to proceed, and the witness is prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll move into closed [as interpreted] session first, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, forgive me, I'll just once again caution you, please, not to mention names because we are now in open session, and the questions I'm going to ask you now probably don't call for any specific names. Very briefly by way of additional background, can you tell the Judges when you recall the Croatian Defence Council or HVO taking over the municipal government in the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when that came about, were there any changes in the way that life was conducted around -- in Vares municipality? And let me just point you to a couple of things. Did anything happen or change concerning telephone service at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we could just use the telephone locally, just in town, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you call such places, for instance, as Sarajevo or Zenica or Tuzla after that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did that continue to be the case up to and including the end of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, too, was another aspect or consequence, if you will, or something that happened after the HVO took over the municipal government, can you tell it the Chamber about any check-points or roadblocks that were set up in Vares municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, at the exit and the entrance into Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you recall where either the Territorial Defence or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the members of those units or those units themselves were located after the HVO took over the Vares municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall after the Vares HVO took over the municipal government where the Territorial Defence or the ABiH units were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Witness, I'm going to jump forward specifically to June 1993, and do you recall any time in June 1993 when a number of Croats came to Vares from Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges just briefly, we're not going to spend a great deal of time on this, but what the impact, what your experience was when these Croats from Kakanj came to Vares? Did it change the way life went on in the town, or did it affect you and your family, again without mentioning any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some provocations. They were taunting the Muslim population in town. At work I had such experience, too, but I tried to ignore it. I tried not to pay any attention to it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me go, then, forward to October of 1993, and again, please, without mentioning any particular names, were you and your family stopped at a check-point sometime in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the it exit, on the way out of Vares at Ponikve. We were going to visit someone, and that's where we were stopped, at the check-point. These were members of the HVO. They wore uniforms. They asked to search the car. They asked what it was that we were carrying. We were bringing some food, and they asked us to take this out. They didn't let us carry this through the check-point. At that moment, a few trucks arrived, Zrinjski. Then Ivica Gavran came in a car, and he didn't talk to me, but we had to wait for him to take over these trucks, and he went after them, and it was only then that they let us go through the check-point, after them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. A couple of follow-up questions, please. When you say that you were carrying some food and this was your -- the car was searched and the food was taken out, can you just briefly tell the Judges: Were the economic conditions and the food that was available in Vares during this time period better than in many other places in Bosnia, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was an abundance of everything, and everything was cheap too. There were big differences in price between Vares and the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. Everything was really cheap in town, in our town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular nickname or way that Vares, the town of Vares, was described during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Oasis of peace."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that some trucks came. You said something about Zrinjski. What did you know, if anything, about what Zrinjski was and what was on these trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a Croat brigade from Tuzla. They were called Zrinjski.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you observe Mr. Gavran -- and that's a name for these purposes I don't think we need to worry about or I would have stopped you. But did you see Mr. Gavran do anything in particular after these trucks passed through the check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He followed them in his car.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, moving forward, then, to the 23rd of October, 1993, or at least the few days before that, can you tell the Judges, as far as you can recall from your own life at that time, did you have any idea, did you see any signals occurring to you or that appeared to you that war -- that the war coming to Vares was imminent at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town was empty. There was no army, no police. Very few citizens were moving about town. It was very unusual. We never believed that any such thing would happen in our town, but -- well, everything was sort of strange.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And approximately how long before the 23rd of October did you see -- you said the town was empty. There was no army, no police. Approximately, as best you can remember, please, how much -- how long was this before the 23rd that you saw these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a week.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Turning to the day of the 23rd of October itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I believe we should go into private session for a couple of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, now with this background in mind, again without mentioning names - you can refer to your mother, you can refer to your father, but not by name - can you tell the Judges, please, what happened on the morning of the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our mother woke us up because she was getting ready to go to work at 6.30 or 7.00, and she was awakened by some kind of noise. She woke me up and she woke my father up. My father went downstairs. At that moment, I walked up to the window and I saw a soldier, armed, in camouflage uniform. I saw him standing in front of our house, and he held a few of our neighbour's at gunpoint. Another soldier was walking out of the house that was near our house with the man who lived there in front of him. This soldier was also in uniform. And the third soldier was walking into our house too. He took the steps. And a few minutes later he took out my father, and they went in the direction of town, all together, from our house. We were lost, afraid. We didn't know what was going on. And we tried to use the phone, because my mother's brother lived in the neighbourhood together with other Muslim neighbours, and I tried to call him. However, the lines were dead that morning. So in this fear we didn't even know what was going on. We tried to pack a few things. We were lost. At that moment we heard shells and gunshots. Then we went down to a neighbour, a lady, who lived below us, and she had a room that was down in a basement, and we thought that we would be safe there. We stayed there even after the alert. And a few hours later, yet again soldiers came. They were armed to -- they came to my neighbour's house. They asked me and my mother to go to our house, and --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. Excuse me. Before we go too much further along, let me ask you a couple of clarifications, please. The soldiers that you say that came to your house and the house of your neighbour on the morning of the 23rd of October, can you tell the Judges of what army or what will military organisation these soldiers were, in terms of what you saw, badges, what you learned at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean what I learned later on or at that moment, what I saw at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That particular -- on the morning of the 23rd were you able to identify from which armed force these soldiers had come or to which force they belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We couldn't recognise them. We couldn't identify them. They weren't our local HVO army. They were from some other municipality. I didn't know any one of them. We didn't know any one of them. They all wore uniforms, camouflage uniforms. They had rifles, knives.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. And your father, and again without mentioning any names, your father and the neighbours that you saw being taken away that morning, can you tell the Court whether -- were men of all nationalities, if I can use that term, or ethnic groups being taken away or only the members of one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were only members of one ethnic group. They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And finally before going forward, you mention that you tried to use the phone. You told us a few moments ago that when the HVO took over Vares municipality in the summer of 1992 that you could not call outside of the town of Vares, and just to be clear, is what you're telling us now is that on the 23rd of October you could not use the phones in Vares town, inside Vares town, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Witness, you had taken us up to the point that you said your father and some of the other men in the area had been taken away, and then you said the soldiers came back sometime later that morning. Can you tell us, if you can, approximately what time the soldiers returned or how much time had passed from the time they took your father away until the time when they came back to your house or to your neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around 10.00. That means that they returned in about three hours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when they returned, and again you started this, but what did they do? Tell us what happened when they returned around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked us to go up to our house, my mother and I. When we entered the house, one soldier in camouflage uniform, he had dark hair, a dark beard, was sitting on the sofa. I had to sit there a bit further away from him. This tall, dark soldier, also in uniform, armed, was standing in the middle of the room. My mother was in front of him. He looked very strange. He had this glassy look as he looked at me, but it seemed as if he was looking through me, as if he couldn't see me. He behaved in a very strange way. Another soldier was there too. He was throwing our clothes out. He was searching our cupboards, our wardrobes. They were looking for more money and jewellery. In the morning they had taken away all our jewellery and money. From my mother's bag, handbag, they took the money that belonged to the store where she worked. There was about 5 or 6.000 Deutschmark there. They were asking for more, and I said that I didn't have any more money, that I only had about 50 or 60 marks in my wallet and that it stayed behind in my private business premises. And I gave them the key, and I asked if they knew where it was, and they said they did. Then the tall, dark soldier took my mother upstairs. The other two were asking questions as in who the cars in front of the house belonged to, and they asked to look at the garage too. We went downstairs. I unlocked the garage. Inside was our car. They asked whether it was all right, and I said that it was being repaired. They tried to start the car, but they couldn't. They asked about the other cars, and I said that they belonged to our neighbours. Then they asked about the building next to our house, yet another shop. I said that this is where a friend worked with our father, and they had some machines there. They wanted to search those premises too. My mother went downstairs followed by this tall, dark soldier. They went inside. They searched the place, then they walked out, and they said something like, "What are you doing to your neighbours?" And we said, "We're not doing anything. We're not doing anything to anybody. We live here. This is our house. We didn't want to go anywhere from our house." And then they asked, "Are you loyal?" I mean, in this fear and feeling so lost, we said yes. We didn't even know what we were saying yes to, but we just wanted to be in agreement with them. And then at the went on as in, "What are your people doing to our people at the front line?" And we were just silent because we had no idea. And then they left the house. We locked the garage, and we went back to our neighbour's, our lady neighbour's. During the night --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You're doing fine. Just let me a couple of questions before you continue on. Just on this question about -- when they asked you are you loyal, was anything said to you or explained to you at the time what they meant by that or loyal to what or to who? Was anything else said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on we assumed that what they meant was when they asked us whether we were loyal to them that meant to the HVO army. I mean, I don't know. We lived there all of us together. We had no problems until then. But in this fear -- I don't know. I mean, we said yes, that we were loyal. We would have done it at any rate.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Let me then go back to where you were. You said that you then left the house. You locked -- your mother locked the garage. Did you return to your neighbour's house at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. And again, please, without mentioning any names, how many people were at the neighbour's house at this time -- by this time? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 14 of us, women and children.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And were all of you Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did the soldiers come back later that day, that is on the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Moving then to the 24th of October, can you tell us whether the HVO soldiers came back to your house or the neighbour's house on that day, the 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the late morning hours, the lady who was our neighbour was airing her sheets in front of the house and she noticed my father and a soldier in front of her house. She walked in and told us about this. We were watching through the window. This man, this soldier in uniform was armed and he held my father at gunpoint. At that moment, another soldier walked out of the empty house that was next door to this house. He went out, and at that moment, I don't know which one of the two, extinguished a cigarette in my father's hand, and then they took him in the direction of our house. Since the keys to the garage and our house were with us, after a while my father came with this soldier to get the keys. He came to our neighbour's house, and he was soaked in blood, his face was, and he was sort of nodding, meaning that he was all right. And then they returned to our house. Then an hour and -- an hour and a half later -- well, actually before that we heard the garage being opened, and we heard them trying to start the car, and then in about an hour, an hour and a half, they left, and then they returned my father to prison. At that moment, the soldiers did not return to us, to the house where we were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one question about that. When you saw your father who had been brought back to the house for the purpose of working on the -- getting the car started, did you know at that time where your father was being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in prison in the school, because this lady who was our neighbour who worked for the Red Cross went on the 23rd to see her husband as well, with another woman, and she saw my father down there at the school, in prison, so we knew where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to now ask to go into private session for some time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, we're moving toward the final part of your testimony it, and we are back in open session again, we please be careful not to say anything that may identify you or your family. Can you tell the Judges, around this time -- in fact, you have mentioned previously today some events in Stupni Do. When do you recall first learning about what had happened in Stupni Do on the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The neighbour who on the 23rd, on Saturday, was in the Red Cross and went to visit her husband in prison and saw my father there, learnt about that from the people in the Red Cross, and later on I learnt about that from my aunt, and -- later on when we came to Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you learn anything more around this time as to -- you said a few moments ago -- you said earlier this afternoon that the HVO soldiers you saw, you did not recognise them as local Vares soldiers, and they were from somewhere else. Did you learn at any time during these days - and by the 24th, 25th - where these soldiers had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came from Kiseljak, and they were the Maturice.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you have taken us to the point, I believe, on Monday, the 25th of October, where you were taken then to a relative's house, did you then at some point come in contact with UNPROFOR about being evacuated to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They evacuated us to Ponikve, where is where their base was, and we were there until -- well, a few days, and then UNPROFOR evacuated us to Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in Dabravine until the 5th of November, and then we went back home to Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about your father during this time, so again I'm just going to caution you. I don't -- I think you can talk about this without being specific as to his identity, but did you learn after coming back into contact with your father what had happened to him during this time, the time that you were staying at the house, or your neighbour's house, and then taken to the UNPROFOR base? Did you find out what had been happening to your father during this same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All we knew was that he was in prison. When we went with UNPROFOR to Ponikve and then Dabravine after that, until the 5th we knew nothing, the 5th of November, that is, whether he was alive, what was happening, until he sent a man to fetch us and take us home, and then we learnt that he was alive and had left prison.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you were reunited then with your father, and thank you for clarifying that, did your father then tell you what had happened to him in the previous several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mistreated. They were beaten. They were psychologically abused too. And the soldiers who locked them up, stood guard over them, they didn't let them go to the toilet. They had to kneel down with their heads down and their hands behind their backs. And as they walked round in a circle they kicked them. Some people kicked more. Others were kicked less. Then if anybody had long hair they would tie their hair up, and they would make people eat their own hair. And when the guards changed and when they were replaced by local people, people from Vares who were in the HVO, then they had access to a doctor, and they behaved much better to them. They were more lenient. They gave them cigarettes to smoke and allowed them to go out to the WC.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me -- sorry, let me stop you there again for a couple of questions before you continue on. You said a moment ago that those were longer hair, their hair would be put up, something to the effect it would be put up and they would be forced to eat their own hair. I'm not sure when you said their hair was put up in some -- was their hair -- were the hair and beards of various prisoners, according to your father, cut or shaved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His beard was shaved and he had short hair, so he didn't have to do that, but many of the others who had longer hair, that's what happened. They cut their hair off and made them eat their own hair.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You just mentioned also that in the first few days of the captivity of your father and these others, the treatment was worse, and then you said the local HVO soldiers came and treatment became better; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever learn, based on anything your father told you or did you learn where the HVO soldiers had come from, the soldiers who had guarded your father and the others for the first several days before the local HVO soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they were from Kiseljak and that they were the Maturice.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did your father -- was your father able to escape from the school sometime on about the 2nd of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did escape on the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did he tell you what happened after that, before you were reunited with him, what had happened between the time that he escaped and the time he was reunited with his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He escaped and then he went into hiding in some hedges and stables or barns. He didn't dare show his face. And then during the night of the 3rd of November he heard over the megaphone appeals made to the Croatian population of Vares to leave town, and the person calling out through this loudspeaker was in a car that circulated around Vares. He didn't know what was going on. And this last the throughout the night. The next day, that would be the 4th, a neighbour came by. He saw him and went to ask him -- he said hello, he greeted him, and then he told him that the town was completely empty, that the soldiers had left, the army had left, and that the army was supposed to come in, and on the 3rd the town was empty. There was no HVO. Most of the Croatian population had left.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did your father tell you around this time that any of the Croat members of Vares, the Croat citizens of Vares, had been forced to leave Vares against their will?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd appreciate if Mr. Scott would not lead on a very important matter like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, without asking the witness about everything she talked about with her father at that time:

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us if your father said anything more -- you said a moment ago that Vares was empty on the 3rd of November. Did you father tell you anything else about the circumstances in which the Croat population left the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the Croatian population had left with the army. Those who didn't want to go, who wanted to stay in town were forced by the HVO to leave town with rifles, and some of them went to the UNPROFOR base at Ponikve, those who didn't want to go, and that's where they stayed until the BH army entered, and then they returned to their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Before we finish, can I just ask you to look at -- we're going to look at three exhibits, please, and it should be -- there's a bundle of exhibits laying there before you. If I can just ask you to look at -- first of all, at P 06092.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6092 did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, on this one, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This particular exhibit, Your Honour, and the questions do not need to be in private session, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But, Witness, if you have that. If you can find that, P 06092, and really it's very -- my question's very limited. Can you please -- and there is a Bosnian language translation of the document which I -- hopefully you have there. I think you have it there in front of you. If you can look at the first page and to the section marked B, toward -- you'll find this -- these words in that passage. In the interest of time I'll just read this you. It says: "However, he confirmed that only male Muslim citizens of Vares were incarcerated in the elementary school and some were beaten when taken to this place." Do you see that? If you look in the -- I think you should have a Bosnian language version there. And if you look -- yes, she has it. I can see you have it. And if you see -- if you go down into the section marked "B. Military situation," and then the -- again, in the Bosnian version, I think if you go about -- perhaps 12 lines down in the text, do you see the sentence that I'm referring to: "However, he confirmed that only male Muslim citizens of Vares ..." You're shaking your head yes, but could you give us a verbal response for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, that information that I just directed your attention to and that I wrote out a moment -- excuse me, read out a moment ago, is that information consistent with what your father had indicated happened to him when he was held -- being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to go to Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I have one or two questions. You remember giving a statement to the Prosecutor's office at the end of August 2003? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after you'd made that statement, it was read over to you in your own language and you were given the opportunity to make any corrections or additions to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when you made that statement in 2003, were you satisfied that that was an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time had already gone by, a certain period of time. Possibly -- possibly I refer to some things in a different way. I tried to forget many things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and I'm not going to ask you about any -- any personal matters today, anything that would be difficult for you. Can we agree, though, that in August of 2003 your memory probably would be a little clearer about the events than it is today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was it the clearest immediately. Well, then.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. By "immediately" you mean right after the events this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the freshest then. As time went by, the years went by, and also the confusion and me wanting to forget things, I did forget some things, or I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement, that's in the English version, you told the Prosecutor that on the 5th of November, Vares was in the hands of the BH army. Do you rather that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We returned on the 5th when the armija was in town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And so any information that you might have had about what happened on the 3rd and 4th of November, that would be information that you heard from your father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you told the Prosecutor that - this is in paragraph 26 - that your father said he heard somebody speaking through a megaphone that all the Croats should leave Vares; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you said, and again I'll quote briefly: "He didn't know what was going on. On Wednesday night, 3 November 1993, it was totally quiet in Vares. On Thursday morning at 7.00, the town was completely empty it. Then my father spoke with a neighbour, and he told him that BH army was coming to Vares. The HVO was withdrawing to Kiseljak." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had already left. There was no army in town, and then the armija came.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, today when you gave evidence, and I'm referring now to page 50 of the transcript, lines 14 to 19, you added a further detail about the Croatian population. You said: "Most of the Croatian population had left with the army. Those who didn't want to go, who wanted to stay in town, were forced by the HVO to leave town with rifles." Now, was that another detail that your father told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I learned that later, after returning to Vares, from people who did not want to leave Vares, who were ethnic Croats, Catholics, and who went to Ponikve, to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But it is true, is it not, that as you told the Prosecutor that by the 5th of November the BH army was in control of Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So it would be consistent with the information that you were given that the Croatian population withdrew from Vares because of the approach of the BH army. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that -- whether that's the reason or whether they were forced by their soldiers to leave town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No. Of course I understand you weren't there yourself. My question is would -- based on the facts you know, that would be a consistent explanation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to leave because they were forced to leave. That is to say their army, the HVO, forced them to leave town, evacuated them. This small part of the population could not be forced to leave Vares. They stayed in their homes or, rather, they went to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you one last thing then. Can we agree that the -- the detail about people being forced to leave Vares with rifles was something that you did not mention to the Prosecutor when you gave your statement in 2003? That was another detail that you've added today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I didn't mention that and if it wasn't written down, then the answer is no. Well, I forget some things. Whenever I try to remember I remember some things, and the other time I'd remember other things, so there would be these variations among my different statements.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That's fine. I -- but just so that we can agree that this is something that you do remember today? Whether or not you remembered it in 2003, this is something that you do remember today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Praljak would have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Witness. I am accused before this court, and quite simply I am speaking in my own name, and it is own proper for me to face the bad things that happened to you too. I'm not going to ask you about that. Heaven forbid. I'm going to ask you about some of the things that the Prosecutor wanted to prove through you. The first matter are telephones in Vares. The Prosecutor asked you whether after the HVO takeover in Vares whether you could phone Zenica, Tuzla, and Sarajevo and your answer was no; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether Sarajevo could phone Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please don't say "but." Just say I know or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you make telephone calls from Zenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about coaxial cables for the transmission of such signals and repeaters and things like that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know under whose control these coaxial cables were between towns, and repeaters, and communication centres of that nature? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know what the last day was when one could make telephone calls from -- from Sarajevo to anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My second question has to do with the Prosecutor's question stating when the people from Kakanj arrived. Tell me, did they come to Vares as a tourist excursion, or were they expelled from Kakanj, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge -- well, I don't know. It's not that they were expelled. It was more a case of them having fled. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You don't know. You stated that in Vares everything was cheap and there was an abundance of everything and that there was an oasis of peace under HVO authority. I'm putting two questions to you. Regardless of the arrival of 15.000 inhabitants of Kakanj who had fled from something to Vares, and that was in June 1993, nevertheless, the situation was good, wasn't it, all the way up to this 23rd of October? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Also, you said that in Vares it was much better than in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, did you go from Vares to Tuzla, Zenica, Busovaca, Vitez? Did you actually know what it was like in other areas so that you could make this kind of comparison, saying that it was, say, better in Vares than it was in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what -- well, while we had some kind of TV programme we could see that in some places there was nothing to eat, whereas in Vares there were all sorts of things, and nothing was expensive at that. Many people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had nothing to eat and had no money to buy anything with, and we had everything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Please, these convoys that brought food into Vares, where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were they coming perhaps from Belgrade, from Sarajevo? Were they airlifts, or do you think that they only could have come from Croatia through Herzegovina and then further north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Just one more thing. In paragraph 5 of your statement - could I please have a look - you said that a week before the 23rd, in Vares there was a kind of ominous peace. So there was this tension, but it was quiet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I would like to read paragraph five where you say: "Seven days before the attack on Stupni Do the town of Vares was completely empty. There was something going on. Nobody was in the cafes or in the streets, even no soldiers. They used to be there but now they had gone. The front linings from Kakanj to Vares were broken. At that time there was some shooting by our BiH army, and the front lines to Kopljari were also broken." Yes. Is this correct what you had stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So according to your statement, is it not the case that seven days before the 23rd, the BiH started attacking this oasis of peace with an abundance of food and everything else, inexpensive? They were attacking the HVO. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just two more things. First of all, your mother, your lady mother had a shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She worked in a shop for someone else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. In Vares throughout this time, did you see any other money but Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian kuna.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Oh, the Croatian kuna was still there. So it could be exchanged for German marks; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There wasn't any other money that came, say, from Sarajevo, from the authorities that were in Sarajevo? There was no money that was printed by the national bank in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. There weren't any Yugoslav dinars either; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't come across any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You didn't come across any. As for the expulsion of the HVO, first question: Did you personally see any soldiers of the HVO threatening Croats to leave town, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about your father? Did he say to you that he had seen a single soldier of the HVO forcing Croats to leave Vares by pointing rifles at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He just heard about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So everything you know about that is what you learned after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina came and after the Croats left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I'm sorry to have bothered you with these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we just have a small correction at 63, 10. The witness said -- when she was speaking about her father, she said that he also hadn't seen such cases, and the transcript says he just heard about this. I think that it's a misunderstanding. I mean, I am sure it's a misunderstanding, so it should be corrected. Do you want to handle this or should I do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you identify a problem, please notify us immediately, because sometimes problems of translation can have grave repercussions if the translation is not proper. So please give the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, in view the fact that we have to check the transcript, and sometimes there are some mistakes, at one point Mr. Praljak asked you whether your father had seen that he had seen with his very own eyes any HVO soldiers forcing Croats with rifles to leave town. What was you ever answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He hadn't seen any such thing. I heard about that later from a lady friend of us who didn't want to leave Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us be quite sure of this. Did your father tell you that he had heard about such things being seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later we did hear about many such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you didn't hear about that from your father, if I understood your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not then, later. We heard about it later. I don't know, a month later, 15 days later, from this lady friend of ours who stayed in Vares, who didn't want to leave. That is what she said to us, that she didn't want to leave her house, and then she stayed back in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And nothing happened to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Witness, good afternoon. I'm going to have a few questions to clarify some details. A moment ago you told General Praljak in response to a question there him about the currency used in Vares, said that in that year, 1993, apart from the German mark there was also the Croatian kuna that was used. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian dinar. The Croatian currency. I don't know whether it was the kuna, but Croatian currency. I don't know exactly what it was called. Perhaps I said kuna because they have the kuna now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did say kuna. All I wanted to ask you was, were you quite sure, because the Croatian kuna as a currency was introduced on the 30th of May, 1994, in actual fact, so that's why I'm asking you whether you're sure it was the kuna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Croatian money, Croatian currency that was used in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, Witness, since -- apart from the statement that you gave to the investigators of the OTP of the Tribunal, we also have your three statements given to institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in none of those statements which were given in 1993 and in 1996 do you mention allegedly forcing -- that the HVO forced the Croats to leave Vares. So I have to ask you the following question: When did you hear for the first time what you told us here today for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we heard that soon after our return from Dabravine, after the 5th. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, the first statement that you gave was given on the 22nd of November, 1993, and what you're saying today you make no mention of at all, not by a single word. So can you tell us whether anybody in any way whatsoever briefed you about what you were to say about that as a witness before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Today our colleague from the Prosecution asked you twice using alternative concepts of Territorial Defence and the BH army, and since in your statement to the OTP of the Tribunal you said quite clearly in paragraph 3 of your statement that the Territorial Defence became the BH army. I would like us to clarify this point and hear whether this happened in mid-1992, and that after mid-1992, all that existed was the BH army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that fact? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly when all this was transformed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you know that there was this transformation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that therefore it is incorrect to say either the Territorial Defence or the BH army, because the Territorial Defence had in fact grown to become the BH army. It had turned into the BH army. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us today that on the 23rd of October, 1993, you were in -- taking shelter and refuge in a neighbour's house, a woman's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that you had taken refuge because there was an alarm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement to the OTP you use the term "general alarm." Do you remember using that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, can you tell us who it was it who sounded the alarm in Vares? Was it the HVO authority that sounded the alarm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time, and we're talking about the 23rd of October, did the HVO have control over Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the 23rd it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know why the alarm was sounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard a few shells falling. There were explosions. We assumed that they were shells, and we saw some sort of -- heard some sort of shooting round town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the shells that you mention, they fell on Vares; right? And that's why the alarm was sounded, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where they actually fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the shells themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did hear them, but we don't know where they fell, whether they fell on Vares or around Vares, in some of the areas surrounding Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that point in time did you have any knowledge whatsoever as to who had targeted these shells to Vares or the surrounding areas, that this was so close that you could hear it? So who shot those shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether upon your return to Vares in November 1993 whether you talked to anybody about those shells and whether you heard who could have done the shooting at Vares on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to anybody, and I don't know. I didn't talk to anybody, and I don't know who shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell it us, please, at that time, did you have any knowledge whatsoever about any combat activities of the BH army in the vicinity of Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Round about that time, yes. During those days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on the basis of what I was able to hear, that there were some -- that there was some fighting around Kopljari.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what general Praljak read out to you a moment ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from that information that you had, was it quite clear that the combat activities on the part of the BH army was directed towards Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the direction was, where they were directed or anything like that. All I know is that there was some fighting going on. Now, whether they went here or the HVO went there, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But you know that on the 3rd of November, the units the BH army entered Vares. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the 3rd, the 5th. The 4th or 5th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remind you what you said in your statement, but it's not essential whether it's the 3rd, 4th, or 5th at this point. You said that on the 3rd they withdrew and that everything was quiet on the 4th and that you returned on the 5th, but it's not an important point. Tell us, please, on that day the 23rd of October, 1993, to the best of your knowledge in Vares were there any members of the BH army who were dressed in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were some Vares inhabitants who were in the BH army, members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they weren't in Vares. They weren't located in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And where were they located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did they visit their families in Vares from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, do you have any knowledge to the effect that in Vares at that time there were collaborators of the BH army, civilians who collaborated with the BH army? So not soldiers but civilians who collaborated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you have any knowledge about the fact that on the territory of Vares, except the Maturice unit that you mentioned, that some other units of the HVO arrived which were not from Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you describe HVO soldiers as people who were doing something, and you don't recognise any -- you said you didn't recognise any local Vares soldiers amongst them, you as a rule say that they were Maturice units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.
