utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you knew that apart from the Maturice unit in the Vares area, other units, other HVO units had arrived, could you then say with any certainty that the soldiers who were not from Vares belonged to the Maturice unit and not perhaps some other HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew -- I was aware that there were the Maturice. Now, I didn't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how did you know that they were the Maturice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everybody mentioned them, spoke about them. Everybody said they were the Maturice from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Everybody said that? You mean when you returned to Kiseljak [sic] in November, 1993? In November 1993, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put something right. I seem to have misspoken and said Kiseljak instead of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when you return to Vares in 1993. That's what I meant to say. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But it would be correct to conclude, would it not, that everything that was not the Vares Brigade, you say, were the Maturice unit members; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you now of a part of your statement from the 1993 statement, the 22nd of November, 1993, in fact, and it is a document provided to us by the Prosecution. It has not been tendered into evidence, and I hope that you will find it in your set of documents and that the Judges will find the document as well. Anyway, you begin your statement with the 22nd of October, 1993, madam, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, did you prepare that document, because I do not have that document, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- we need to make sure that this is erased from the transcript or whatever we end up doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. We need a redaction, please, on line -- page 71, line 8. And please -- please, I advise counsel, please be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please prepare an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise, and I propose that we move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Kovacic wanted to take the floor to raise an issue related to translation. I'd like to say that the audio recording is the actual record of this trial, so you can always refer to the audio recording if you find a discrepancy between the audio recording and the transcript, either in French or in English, and then you can make corrections if need be. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I was sure I pushed it. [Interpretation] As you know, Your Honour, for the week of the 2nd of April, starting with the 2nd of April and all the days during the week, we have a witness, he's an ambassador. I won't state his name out of an abundance of caution, there might be some protective measures in place. As far as I know, there aren't, but he is a respected ambassador from the 4th -- from the 2nd right through the week, and he's an important witness. And the Prosecutor with that witness plans to use two documents. One document is and handwritten diary in English, a personal diary, personal document composed of nine parts, nine P numbers, and has a total of almost 800 pages, 798 pages, and the Prosecution - and we discussed this - plans to provide translations into the B/C/S. We have some 26 pages already, and my colleagues from the Prosecution say that another 100 pages are due to arrive shortly. Now, with respect to that diary, which is certainly a relevant and important document because it's an extensive one and very important, my proposal is that the Prosecution issues an order that the whole document is disclosed in the B/C/S translation, because there are portions inside which the Defence can use to its advantage, and if the Prosecution takes one section we might need another section. I think that it is the right of the accused to have that. I don't see that there is -- that is a right that has been established. There are no two ways about it. It is an important exhibit, and we did -- never wanted to split hairs. We didn't insist upon minor matters, but this is too important to be ignored. And along with that, and this is my second proposal, the Prosecution proposes to use the presidential records, the president of the Republic of Croatia, five minutes from -- with five P numbers, which in total in the Croatian language, in the original, have 265 pages. They are 265 pages long. But the Prosecution has provided excerpts from those records and minutes. Some have been translated, a total of 87 pages, and with respect to this document it is my proposal that the Prosecution should provide the entire translation in English for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and for those who do not speak Croatian, the Defence counsel, because we need the integral text. You know that meetings deal with different topics. You have been able to see some of them. And very often the discussion or debate begins on some pages and then they go back to that same discussion later on. So it's impossible to extract just a few sentences or a few pages. So we would like to appeal that we be provided with the entire translation, but I would particularly like to insist upon the first translation with regard to the diary. The accused have the right to see the exhibits in a language they understand, and that the exhibits that the indictment relies on and the Prosecution relies on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. We have indeed discussed this with our colleague, Mr. Kovacic, during a couple of the breaks yesterday and today. Perhaps this might be an issue that we could come back to on Thursday in some greater detail, but let me just for now indicate what we have been provided with by Ambassador Okun are hundreds, and I'm talking about more than 700 pages of his handwritten diaries covering a period from October 1991 until May of 1993. We have gone through these diaries and provided translations of the excerpts of those diaries which we believe are relevant and which we will attempt to tender into evidence when this witness comes and testifies. The short answer is that to provide -- and I should also indicate that some of those translations are still in process, and we will disclose those as soon as they are available. At this point in time, it is simply not possible to provide translations of hundreds of pages of diary material when neither party has identified that as exhibits to be exhibited before the Trial Chamber. We don't have the resources to do that, and that would most definitely cause a delay and/or cause Ambassador Okun to come back for cross-examination. Our position is very clear, that clearly with respect to materials that we want to use as exhibits, we will provide translations of those, either documents or excerpts of documents in case of lengthy documents. I should also indicate that it's my understanding that these diaries were used in the Krajisnik and Milosevic cases without full translations being -- being required. These diaries of Ambassador Okun have featured in a number of cases and, to date, no Trial Chamber has ever required the Prosecution to create full transcripts of these diaries. I would also point out that -- that the jurisprudence of this institution is very clear with respect to statements. Clearly these diaries are not statements falling within the scope of the rules that would require the Prosecution to provide B/C/S translations of those written diaries. I will distinguish this situation from that which we had with respect to an earlier witness, whose name I will not mention, but whose entire diary became an exhibit, in which case we did produce a -- a translation of the entire diary. You will recall that that witness came back for purposes of cross-examination. That's a very different situation where the entire diary is being tendered into evidence. As I've indicated, Ambassador Okun's diary covers periods prior to the indictment period, number one; and number two, it is more than 700 pages long. And my understanding is that we have selected the excerpts of that and those excerpts have either been translated and disclosed or are being -- in the process of being translated and will be disclosed as soon as those excerpts are available. And if it would be helpful, I can again cite the Trial Chamber to a decision of the Appeals Chamber that clearly indicates the definition of a statement, and it is clear, in our submission, that the handwritten diaries of this witness are not statements which would require the full translation thereof. Of course if any of the Defence teams want to use excerpts other than those which the Prosecution is proposing to tender, they are fully at liberty to either produce their own translations of those excerpts or to request CLSS to produce translations of those excerpts. And again, perhaps this might be an issue that we want to, or one of the parties, wants to come back to on Thursday when we'll have a little bit more time to discuss any of these outstanding procedural or evidentiary matters. I do have a witness standing by to begin his testimony. I believe we can finish that witness's testimony this evening, and I would propose that we do that rather than -- than run the risk of having the witness not complete his testimony today with respect to this matter, which can be dealt with and resolved in a couple of days' time anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will think about this, think about what Mr. Kovacic said. On the 13th of July in 2006, we rendered a decision about the evidence and paragraph 5 of the decision states, "the admission of an excerpt of an exhibit is not excluded on the only basis that the entire exhibit has not been tendered into evidence. When the opposing party states that the excerpt takes on a different meaning within the entire context of the exhibits, that party has to demonstrate its assertion. If the party wants to discuss the other excerpts at the hearing, it has to provide the necessary translations." So we dealt with this matter before. We'll deal with it again tomorrow during our daily meeting, and we'll tell you whether we'll deal with this during the special hearing dedicated to the issue raised by Mr. Karnavas. But this is a different matter. So we'll think about the matter and we'll tell you what we think tomorrow. As far as I'm concerned, I know perfectly well what I want to do, but I'm not alone. I have colleagues next to me, and we'll deal with this tomorrow. We're now going to bring in the next witness, and I'm returning the decision to the legal officers. No protective measures for the next witness if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Good evening, Your Honours; good everybody in the courtroom. There are no protective measures for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come, going back to the previous witness, I will be tendering the entire -- all of his diaries in because of the aspect of the joint criminal enterprise. It's historical in nature. It gives a continuity of what was happening in the break-up of Yugoslavia, in the negotiations that followed, and also I -- just very briefly, I think that the Defence is going to require about four days of cross-examination of this gentleman. I'm saying this right now. He's an important witness, and I think to assume that one party can do a cross-examination in one hour is really unrealistic, given the nature of what he's going to be talking about and the extent of his notes, because I think the notes are very, very important. These are notes while he was taking -- he was basically the secretary for Vance-Owen during those meetings so that's why I mention it. But we can discuss this at some other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've taken note of what you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you please stand up because now I have to ask you to take the solemn declaration. Can you please give me your last name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mufid Likic. I was born on the 27th of August, 1969 in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I'm unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before a court of law about the events that took place in your country or is it the first time that you're testifying about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the proceedings against Dominik Ilijasevic that are still ongoing. I'm a witness there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read out the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Let me give you some information. You will now answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. The Prosecution have decided that they need about 30 minutes to ask you a number of questions and to show you a number of documents. Following this, the Defence will have one hour and a half - that's been decided by the Chamber - will have one hour and a half, that may be too much, to put questions to you, and you have to answer his questions, both from the Prosecution and the Defence. At any time the Judges sitting before you can put questions to you, but now we refer to wait for both parties to have put questions to you before asking questions. If at any time you do not feel well, please tell us immediately that it is the case, and since we won't have time to complete your testimony today, you will have probably to come back tomorrow. Let me now give the floor to the Prosecution for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Likic.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mufid Likic is a 92 ter witness and his testimony is relevant to paragraphs 207, 208, and 210 of the indictment, and I will first give a summary of his written statement. I'll read out the Rule 65 ter summary. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim man from Stupni Do. In 1993, the Croatian Democratic Union, Croatian Defence Council, held the power in Vares. The mayor of Vares, a Muslim woman, was no longer allowed to perform her function and was forced to leave. On 30 August, 1993, the witness was arrested and taken to an HVO military prison in Vares. He was beaten and interrogated about Stupni Do and how many ABiH soldiers were there -- there were. The next morning, the witness was taken to a civilian police station and again interrogated. The witness escaped but spent several days in hospital because of his injuries. On 18 October 1993, on the way from Breza towards Stupni Do, the witness and five other Muslim men were arrested at an HVO check-point. For the next several days they were held in three different locations in Vares, including the police station and the steel factory. They were beaten and interrogated at all locations. During his detention in the steel factory, the witness could see that Stupni Do was burning and under attack. Witness was also held in the secondary school where there were many more civilian Muslim males. During an UNPROFOR visit, about 25 detainees who were in the worst condition were hidden. Two soldiers visited the witness during his detention. One of them said he was slaughtered -- that he had slaughtered Ramiz Likic, in Stupni Do. They fired shots over the detainees' heads and tortured the men. The next day the witness was in such bad condition that he had to be taken to the hospital in Vares-Majdan and the next day to the hospital in Vares. Ivica Rajic and Leon Dodik came to the hospital. Dodik recognised the witness and told Ivica Rajic he was a Muslim. Rajic said, "Slaughter him and throw his corpse in the river Stavnja -- Stavnija [as interpreted]." After they left the witness beg the doctors to help him. He and another Muslim man were taken to the UNPROFOR base in Ponikve. That concludes my 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about your written statement. Is it correct that you provided a written statement to the offices of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on 28 October 1998, and the 1st of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at that time that you -- that you provided this written statement did you answer the questions to the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you ask -- did you answer these questions freely, that is, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that interview, was the statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you then sign that statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, with the assistance of the usher I'm going to now show you your statement. Now, if you can take a look at Exhibit number 09883, and -- which starts with the English version of your statement, and could I ask you to confirm whether the signature on this statement is indeed your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when you met with an investigator and myself you were given an opportunity to review your statement in the Bosnian language and to make any corrections or clarifications if necessary. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that you then had a couple of corrections and clarifications that you wanted to make -- wanted to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, to save some time, what I will do is -- is, I will reach -- for each correction I will -- or clarification, I will read it out, and maybe then you can confirm whether that's, in fact, the correction or clarification that you wanted to make. The first one is in the fourth paragraph of page 4 of the English statement which reads: "Because he was an invalid -- invalid, Resad would not be able to walk with us to Stupni Do, and therefore he would drive back to Breza." Now, is it correct that this sentence, especially in the B/C/S version, may be interpreted as if Resad Likic was not arrested on the 18 October 1993 but, however, that he was in fact arrested together with the other men that were stopped at that time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: It was written there that he was supposed to come back in order to come back to Breza. That is what we thought, that he should come back to Breza because he was a disabled person, but we didn't get to the village of Breza where we were supposed to come back, and he was arrested together with us, and we came by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, maybe -- maybe I'll -- it's -- I can refer to you -- to your statement in the B/C/S language on page 5. You will find the B/C/S statement there as well. And if you could go to page 5 of your statement, and -- and about the fourth paragraph just below -- about -- just below the middle of the page there is a sentence which reads in full, and in the English version it's on page 6, the second full paragraph where you mention the name of four other Muslims who were detained with you in the same room at the steel factory. Now, is it correct that yesterday you stated that one name was omitted there, and could you give us which name was omitted, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cizmo, Mujo. He was there, too. Nedzad Cazimovic is written down here. Fahrija Balta, Semso Ibrisimovic, Besim Paralangaj, but Cizmo, Mujo is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I refer you to page 6 of your statement and the second line from the top. There is a sentence which reads as follows: "When Ahmed did not react he cut off one of his ears." Is there something you want to say about this particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Ahmed didn't react, I wanted to say that he had cut his ear a bit with a knife, not that he cut it off completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I again refer you to page 6, and this is near the bottom of the third full paragraph. There is a sentence which reads: "Plecic carried me to the UNPROFOR unit who then transported me to their compound in Ponikve, situated in the outskirts of Vares." What did you want to say about this particular sentence, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that Enes Plecic, who was with me, was just as beaten up as I was and that he couldn't carry me. This doctor who took us out of the hospital brought us exactly to UNPROFOR in a car because it was the UNPROFOR people who were on -- the women and children. And he came right there to them. They took me from the vehicle and transported me to their own transporter. So Enes was as beaten up as I was, so he certainly couldn't carry me, whereas here it says that he's the one who carried me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, besides these clarifications and corrections that you've just made, are there any other corrections or clarifications you want to make to your written statement?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: No, I read it twice. I think that's it. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to look now at Exhibit 08850, which is also in that bundle. Witness, this is a list of names, and is it correct that yesterday in proofing you went through this list of names?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, what I would like you to do today in court is again through this list of names and identify the names of the persons of whom you know that they were detained with you in the various detention centres that -- that you -- that you were in -- in this period of October 1993. So what I'm only -- I'm only interested in the names of the persons who you can confirm were also detained at the time you were also detained in either the secondary school or the steel factory. So maybe if you can go through the list and then mention the number and then -- and tell us in which detention centre that person was with you.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Number 2, Edin Galiba Adanalic. When they transferred me to the hospital, to the emergency ward there, they had already brought him there. He was already there because he had sustained serious injuries. 24, Fahrija Balta.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where was this person detained?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: In the steel mill. The ones I'm going to read out were all in the steel mill, together with me. 40, Nedzad Cazimovic; 43, Salem Cerenic; 90, Semsudin Ibrisimovic; 122, Ibrahim Karic; 144, Jakub Likic, my brother; 148, Esref Likic; 149, Resad Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you also see your own name? You may -- may have not -- is your own name also on this list?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't want to point that out. That's 143. I think that was unnecessary, but there you go, 143. 153, Himzo Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, before we turn to the -- to the next page, could I ask you again a question about number 122, because you've -- you've told us that these were all prisoners that -- that were with you at -- in the steel factory. Is the person you mentioned under 122, was he one of the prisoners with you in the steel factory?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: No, sorry. Ibrahim Karic was in the secondary school, in the gym there. I remember him because he was a big man, corpulent, strong, physically strong. They took him out to beat us, you know, the rest of us. If he wouldn't do it, then they would beat him, so the man had to do it. I remember that. And therefore I apologise for having included his name among those who were at the steel mill. 192, Besim Paralangaj; 219, Fikret Selman; 239, Meho Trklja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That is it?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: That's it. Well, yes, as for what I can be sure of those are the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am going to ask the usher it take the witness out of the courtroom very briefly, but I have to do this, and then I'll ask the registrar to move into private session. Sir, you will have to leave the courtroom for a few minutes, and then you'll come back. It will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While we're waiting, if I may make one observation in order to speed up the process. Obviously in a case like this where the gentleman has looked at a list of names and has gone over the names with the Prosecutor, it makes no sense to then have the witness try to spot them on the -- you know, when they've already done this already in the proofing session. I mean, it gives the illusion, somehow, that now the witness is doing it fresh from his memory. Therefore, given that it's merely an illusion and we're not in front of a jury, it makes sense for the Prosecutor to simply just lead the witness and say yesterday in a proofing session when I showed you the list you identified X, Y, and Z, and so on and so forth. I think that would be, in my opinion, a better way to -- to proceed, if indeed they've gone over the list, because there are no secrets at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a very interesting suggestion. It's up to the Prosecution to apply it, and that would indeed save a lot of very precious time. It's now for the Defence to conduct the cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, we have no questions for the gentleman. We wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Praljak would have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Mr. Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 3 of the Croatian version of your statement in one, two, three, four, five -- fifth paragraph from the bottom, you said that on the 18th of October, 1993, you were in your uncle's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say that Himzo Likic was there, too, commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Stupni Do unit.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Jakub Likic, member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Stupni Do unit?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my brother.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Esref Likic, commander of the battalion in Breza, near Bosnia-Herzegovina. Resad Likic, former member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he stepped on a mine and became an invalid, and Ahmed Likic member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Stupni Do unit?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you say all were dressed in civilian clothes except for Esref who was wearing camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, were there quite a few people in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who often wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning until the army was established; of course, they did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you say in the beginning here a reference is made to the 18th of October, and you say out of six or seven men everybody wore civilians clothes except for Esref. So do we agree that the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina then, in Vares and around Vares, very often wore civilian clothes as though they were members of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. And you say for the very same day, a few lines down, that a man in BH army uniform walked in as you were sitting there, and he took Himzo out and spoke with him for a while.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When Himzo came back he told us that they had to go to Stupni Do because the situation was getting worse and there were -- there was already fighting going on between the HVO and the BH army around Vares, especially in an area called Lijesnica. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That fighting around Vares started -- or, rather, around Lijesnica started around the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was the date, but if that's what I wrote then that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Was Lijesnica in that direction from where the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was coming, the one that was stationed in Zenica -- or, rather, the 3rd Corps - sorry - stationed in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: How can I know? I was not the corps commander, sir, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm not insisting on anything.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You say further on that this man who informed you about the fighting having started, you say he told us that the man who visited him and spoke to him was the chief of staff of the army BH brigade of Vares. Do you know that the Bosniaks, the Muslims from Vares, had their own brigade which was a regular brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Regular brigade, they had it when the army took Vares. That's when it was the regular brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about earlier on? You say here that the chief of staff of the brigade of Vares of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Perhaps that's what they called it, brigade, but it wasn't a brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: No, no. He was outside with him. I personally did not see the man, and they talked when they took him outside.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know what the number of that brigade was and whether it had a name, the brigade of the BH army composed of Bosniaks Muslims from Vares, that is.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: The 122nd Brigade, I think. I think that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it the 322nd or the 122nd?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: The 322nd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know whether that brigade, the 322nd Brigade, attacked Vares together with the other units of the BH army from the 2nd and 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there then. I was in hospital. I was in Breza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In talking to the people you knew later on, did you receive any information to the effect that that brigade, the 322nd, composed of Bosniaks from Vares, took part in the attack on Vares?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that you were received by a Croatian doctor and despite risk to him sent you to hospital where there were 15 other wounded Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, and I would like to say thank you to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And on page 6, on page 6 you also confirm -- you say underneath that: "I spent the rest of day in that department and the following night, and the next morning we were able to see and hear that there was fighting going on from the direction of Mount Perun, and it seemed that the BH army was attacking the HVO from its positions." Now, do you confirm that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know that the HVO as it was from the arrival of the people from Kakanj, from June, or the arrival of the people from Kakanj, until the 18th of October succeeded in preserving an oasis of quiet, of calm in Vares, as witnesses said, until the attack started, regardless of the problems that occurred with so many refugees, right up to the 18th -- 17th, 18th of October when the BH army started to attack Kopljari and take control of it, and that they had three dead, two wounded and so on? Do you know that at that time there was law and order, relatively speaking, with enough food and everything else in Vares up until that time?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: As to enough food, sir, if you turn over to the second page and read about this oasis of peace on the 30th of August and what it says, I said I was with Adisa Likic, Edina Kadric, and Almedina Lukovic [as interpreted] in a cafe called Mak in Vares-Majdan. I intended to buy a truck and, for that purpose, I had four and a half thousand Deutschmarks. I would just like to refer to that oasis of peace, as you said it. I was arrested in that oasis of peace and they took away my four and a half thousand Deutschmarks and my health. And I spent all the rest of the time in the hospital in Breza, in that oasis of peace and calm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, I will be asking you the questions and would you kindly answer them. I'm not trying at all to deny what happened to you individually, personally. Now what I asked you about the oasis of peace is something that witnesses testified to here in this court who belong to your own nationality or ethnic group. I didn't imagine this, think this up. I wasn't in Vares but I'm talking about the general state of affairs, not what happened to you, and it is with regret that I learn what happened to you, but who took part in the knowledge that you had four and a half thousand Deutschmarks. This is something that the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina must establish, which unfortunately isn't doing that, and I'm asking you about the overall situation regardless of the very ugly and terrible personal fates that you individually suffered. I don't want to contest that at all. So I'm asking you once again: After the arrival of the 15.000 people from Kakanj who were expelled in June 1993, up until the 18th of October of that same year in Vares, generally speaking, without taking into account the terrible situation you yourself were in, what -- would you say that the situation was tolerable with a view to food, that it was a relatively calm, that kind of calm can exist in a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was peaceful, but there wasn't enough food because whatever we went to buy in Vares we had to wait and they were -- policemen were waiting for us at Stupni Do. We men wasn't -- weren't able to go down to Vares and the women had to make do and go to Breza and take the food. Now as far as shooting is concerned, there wasn't any of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need to ask you anything else. Thank you for answering my questions and for coming here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Witness, good afternoon. With respect to a statement made by General Praljak and the question he asked you -- the question that was asked you, and he said that he wouldn't go into the fact that four and a half thousand German marks were taken away from you, I would just like to see if what you say in your statement in that respect is correct, that you received a receipt for the money that was taken away from you by the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Witness, on the 18th of October, 1993, you were arrested when, with a group of your compatriots, you were going from the direction of Breza towards Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that day, were you a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to remind you of your statement, or more exactly your testimony of the 31st of May, 1996, and it is --.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I'd like to draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that it is a document provided to us by the Prosecution which was not envisaged as an exhibit in this -- these proceedings, and it is an interview of this witness held on the 31st of May, 1996, with the investigating judge of the higher court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, on that occasion you said and the first sentence of your statement is as follows: "I was a member of the BH army." That's how you start off.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army from the 13th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, this is what you said, sir: "I was a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army but in the Vares-Majdan cafe, a cafe when I -- where I was wearing civilian clothes on the 30th of August, 1993. I was arrested and they beat me for two days, and seven days later I had to spend time in hospital." So you're talking about August 1993, and before the Sarajevo court you said that at that time you were a member of the BH army. Can you tell us whether you were telling the truth, testifying to the Sarajevo court?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I told the truth but perhaps it was understood in a different way. They asked me whether I was a soldier, so I was a soldier from the 13th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell me, please, if you were not a member of the BH army why then do you emphasise the fact that you were wearing civilian clothing? Because if you weren't a soldier that would be quite normal. You would normally be wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: When I gave this statement, the investigator asked me whether I was in civilian clothes, because he knew that all the rest were members of the BH army, and just Esref was wearing a military uniform. All the others were wearing civilian clothes because they had come to visit me in the hospital, because -- well, I was not in -- I was in hospital by the uncle [as interpreted]. And I had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were ill on that same day when, from Breza, you were moving towards Stupni Do, that same day; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, in your statement, in the Croatian version it is on page 3, and it's roughly in the middle of the page, towards the lower half of the page, you say: "Because of the injuries that I sustained due to the beating during the interrogation, I had to stay in hospital for seven days in Breza. After that, that is to say after hospital, I was not able to return to Stupni Do because the relations between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in the area of Vares were not particularly good. I learnt about the tensions from my cousins from Stupni Do," and that is why you stayed with your relatives in Breza; right? So explain to us, Witness, what tension was there? What was that all about, and why did your relatives advise you not to go back to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Already at that time when I was down there, the HVO of Vares had already made an ultimatum once to the unit in Stupni Do to hand over their weapons, and the people had already moved out once, the elderly and the women, and so the people advised me not to go there because it wasn't any good up there, and then the people returned, and they were there in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness added -- "prior to the genocide," the interpreter heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was an HVO demand by which the military unit of the BH army in Stupni Do should hand over weapons. That's what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the Trial Chamber would like to know whether the other Defence counsel have questions for the witness, because we are looking at the clock. One of my colleagues would like to have a question -- to ask a question. Ms. Tomic, would you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll certainly need 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need any time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it was these tensions, those tensions. Now, this unit of the BH army which you mention now in Stupni Do, how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: About 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the inhabitants of Stupni Do and the military unit of the BH army in Stupni Do, this request by the HVO to hand over their weapons, did they understand this as a threat of some kind or not?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, of course they took it at a threat, and that's why they told me not to go there. The people didn't want to hand over their weapons, and then they thought that a conflict would erupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in expecting conflicts did they build trenches, prepare themselves for a defence, strengthen their BH army unit in Stupni Do, reinforced it, which would be logical if one expects a conflict to break out?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to how many new forces arrived to Stupni Do to help out the BH army in preparation for a defence in a possible conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were the units of the BH army ready, for example, from Breza, that in the case of a conflict they should move towards Stupni Do straight away?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. It would be logical. Now, whether they did, well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that tomorrow, analysing the plans of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, but I'll make use of my five minutes to analyse this statement of yours in greater depth. On the 18th of October, in Breza, you found yourself there with people from the unit -- units of the -- Stupni Do, from the battalion in Breza. Can you tell us how many members the battalion in Breza had?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: How should I know how many soldiers the battalion in Breza had?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then the chief of staff of the Vares Brigade of the BH army arrived. Can you tell us how many members that brigade had?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you're asking me that. How I would know how many soldiers a brigade numbered?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you go on to say in your statement that Himzo told you to set out with him in order to take some relatives out of Stupni Do. Can you tell us what you meant by taking out relatives from Stupni Do, and what was all this about on the 18th of October, 1993? What could that have been? What could it have meant? Why? What were the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that it was a village under siege, encircled, and that, if anything happened, that there would be a massacre because it's a small village under siege with few fighters, little weapons, and that meant that somebody ought to take the people out of the village to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm interested in, precisely. So the plan was to evacuate the civilian population from the village in order to avoid a possible, as you -- the term you used, massacre.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague has told me that the answer given by the witness on line 22, page 99, was not recorded, so can I just take a moment to see where that was and what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question to you was whether you have any knowledge about units of the BH army who came to Stupni Do in order to prepare the defence in the case of a possible conflict, and now your answer wasn't recorded. So would you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, not a single man came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that last question of mine was whether there were any plans on the part of the BH army for the civilian population of Stupni Do to be evacuated in order to prevent what you termed a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was that a plan for the evacuation of the whole population?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: It was a plan to evacuate the elderly people and children, you know, because there were people who were sick and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the fact that the people who were supposed to be evacuated, you didn't mention the women among those people, leads me to conclude that the women in Stupni Do had their wartime assignments, war tasks. Can we agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: No. In Stupni Do they had the task and assignment --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To defend Stupni Do; right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, the three women working in the kitchens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should not interrupt the witness to tell him what he has to tell you when you ask a question, as you just did. But I think the time's up for today anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think you're able to follow the course of our question and answer in B/C/S, because the witness made a slight pause. Now, that pause, I used to ask this additional question. Otherwise, it wasn't my intention to interrupt the witness, and I know it's not proper to do that, and I never do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It's 7.00 p.m. We'll reconvene tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
